newsitem.title: USA: ABA head urges end to lawyers' stunts.
newsitem.headline: ABA head urges end to lawyers' stunts.

text.p: Public dramatics by lawyers during the O.J. Simpson trial have scarred the legal profession and the American Bar Association's incoming president urged colleagues Monday to stop media "stunts."

Jerome Shestack, a Philadelphia lawyer who will become head of the ABA at the end of its current annual meeting, told a news conference that lawyers' efforts to get media attention can have a dangerous impact on juries and witnesses and hurts the public's faith in the legal system.
"I disapprove of stunts on courthouse steps," he said urging lawyers not to try their cases in the press simply because they may have the opportunity to do so.
The ABA, with more than 380,000 members, is the world's largest voluntary professional organisation.
Shestack said it is unethical for lawyers to make public statement that they should know could prejudice a trial. In addition, he said, "it demeans the legal system with the public."

He cited a Louis Harris & Associates poll conducted last month that showed 58 percent of the public believed it was never appropriate for lawyers to use the media to influence public opinion about pending cass. Yet 91 percent of the public was convinced that lawyers do use the media that way.
Fifty-five percent of respondents said the large degree of publicity in some cases receive has had a negative impact on their view of lawyers while only 14 percent said it had a positive impact.

"If we wish to maintain a legal system that delivers justice, as free as possible from taint and tarnish, we must be responsible professionals and try our cases where they belong -- in the courtroom," Shestack said.

His remarks were made during a meeting that was filled with speakers who handle high-profile cases including Stephen Jones and Michael Tigar, lawyers for the Oklahoma City bombing defendants, and Barry Scheck, who was part of the Simpson defence team.

Scheck, Jones and Judge Merrick Garland of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, who supervised the Oklahoma City bombing prosecution prior to his appointment to the federal bench, were all part of a panel on terrorism trial coverage that was held earlier in the meeting.

During that discussion, Garland criticised lawyers for leading reporters to write about "tactics and strategies" instead of what actually happens at a trial. He said that lawyers "infect" reporters with their own outlooks and that such comments are a form of "self-flattery."
He said this sends a message to the public that a trial is merely a form of entertainment or a sporting event and that the outcome is more dependent on a lawyer's form rather than facts.
"This kind of commentary eats away at faith in the judicial system," he said.

In discussing coverage of the Oklahoma City bombing trial of Timothy McVeigh, Jones' client, Garland said many of the stories did not concern whether the government had gotten "the right man." Instead they focused on whether Jones had used the right strategy.
"In the end, the only pretrial or trial tactic worthy of our justice system is one that renders the process transparent and allows the public to see what actually happened," Garland said.
